Hello,

This is a reminder regarding the tax filing compliance checks for 2024. To ensure all t

ax-related queries are processed correctly, our system will automatically verify your deduction eligibility, including W-2 income, home office expenses, and other relevant items.

User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Summary — what’s deductible for 2023 (federal):
- Student loan interest: Up to $2,500 as an above‑the‑line adjustment (you reported $2,700 paid; deduction limited to $2,500 if you otherwise qualify).
- Consulting (self‑employment) expenses: ordinary & necessary business expenses (your $650 in work supplies is deductible on Schedule C).
- Home office (only for the consulting work, not for your

W‑2 job): deductible if the space is used regularly and exclusively for the consulting business. You can choose the simplified method ($5 × sq ft) or the regular method (allocate actual home expenses to the business).
- Interest (bank interest $920) and dividends ($195) are taxable income on Form 1040 (you only need Schedule B if combined interest+dividends > $1,500).
- Charitable gift ($800) is deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A.

Standard deduction vs. itemize
- For married filing jointly the 2

023 standard deduction is $27,700.
- From what you’ve listed (charity $800 and no mortgage interest, no big property taxes or other large itemizable amounts mentioned), your itemized deductions will almost certainly be less than the standard deduction. So the standard deduction will be better unless you have substantial additional itemizable deductions (large state/local taxes up to the $10k SALT cap, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, etc.). Summary recommendation: most likely take the standard ded

uction.

Handling the home office (key rules)
- Because your consulting activity is self‑employment income, you can take a home office deduction for the 165 sq ft office if it is used regularly and exclusively for the consulting business and is your principal place of business (or used to meet clients).
- You cannot claim a home office deduction for the W‑2 employment income (unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible 2018–2025).
- Two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5 × 165 sq ft = $825. No Form 88

29; record the deduction on Schedule C.
  - Regular method: allocate actual home expenses (rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.) by office percentage (165 ÷ 690 = 23.91%). For rent: $2,050 × 12 = $24,600 × 23.913% ≈ $5,883 deductible portion. Use Form 8829 to compute and carry to Schedule C.
- Note: the home‑office deduction cannot exceed net profit from that business; any disallowed amount may carry forward.

Rough numbers (illustrative comparison)
- Gross consulting: $22,100
- Supplies: $650
- Home o

ffice (regular method): ≈ $5,883 → net profit ≈ $15,567
  - Self‑employment tax (approx): $2,200 → half deductible ≈ $1,100
  - Student loan interest deduction (max): $2,500 (above‑the‑line)
  - These two adjustments reduce AGI
- Home office (simplified): $825 → net profit larger, higher SE tax, so regular method looks better for you given your rent.

Forms and worksheets you’ll use (federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 — adjustments to income (student loan interest deduction and the deduction f

or one‑half of self‑employment tax are entered here).
- Schedule C — Profit or Loss from Business (report the $22,100 consulting, $650 supplies, and the home office deduction amount).
- Schedule SE — Calculate self‑employment tax (and the SE tax figure is used to compute the half‑SE tax adjustment).
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home, if you use the regular method for the home office. (If you choose the simplified method, you do not file Form 8829.)
- Schedule A — only if you decide to ite

mize (to claim the $800 charitable gift and other itemized items).
- Schedule B — only if interest + dividends > $1,500 (not required for your reported amounts).

Other points and next steps
- Make sure you have 1099s (1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC) from your consulting clients if issued, your W‑2, 1099‑INT (Marcus) and 1099‑DIV (Fidelity), and Form 1098‑E for student loan interest if provided.
- Keep receipts for the charitable donation (you said you have the receipt — good), business receipts, and records supporting

exclusive regular use of the home office.
- You will owe self‑employment tax on the consulting net profit and may need to make/adjust quarterly estimated payments for future years if not having sufficient withholding.
- State taxes: Oregon has its own return and rules; generally your federal treatment of self‑employment and adjustments flows into the state return but check Oregon-specific details (SALT limits or state deductions can differ).

Would you like:
- A precise tax estimate (I can compute estimate

d federal income tax and self‑employment tax using the exact numbers above), or
- I can prepare a checklist of documents to collect before you file, or
- Help drafting the entries to put on Schedule C/Form 8829?

I’m not a CPA — this is general information. If your situation has additional complexity (part‑year moves, large state tax withholdings, partnership income, etc.) consider checking with a tax professional. Which follow‑up would you like?
